abstract: This study characterizes the proteomic responses of adipose-derived mesenchymal stromal cells (ASC) to novel compounds that target the interaction between pigment epithelium-derived factor (PEDF) and the 37 KDa Laminin Receptor (LR). Building on previous research, we introduced the second-generation analog, 02–09, for comparative analysis with C3, the original compound. C3 was identified through in silico screening and experimental validation, showing anti-inflammatory activity. Analog 02–09 was synthesized by modifying C3's aromatic ring, resulting in similar binding affinities to LR. The distinct molecular effects of C3 and 02–09, along with their potential as anti-inflammatory therapies from prior work, suggested their multi-functional utility. Proteomic profiling of ASC, under both undifferentiated and chondrogenic differentiation conditions, was performed using LC-MS/MS, with controls including the PEDF-derived peptide p18 and the cartilage-regenerative compound Kartogenin (Krt). Both C3 and 02–09 induced significant proteomic modulation compared to controls, with enrichment in pathways related to integrin β1 signaling, extracellular matrix (ECM) organization , and TGF-β signaling . C3 uniquely activated the nuclear receptors meta-pathway, whereas 02–09 was associated with laminin interactions . Protein-protein interaction and transcription factor enrichment analyses revealed distinct and overlapping regulatory networks for LR-targeting compounds. During chondrogenic differentiation, C3 primarily enhanced proteins linked to a chondrogenic phenotype with minimal fibrogenic activity, while 02–09 showed an influence on both chondrogenic and fibrogenic pathways. Comparative analysis of the proteomic response to C3 or 02–09 with a single-cell RNA-sequencing dataset confirmed that C3's modulated proteins primarily correlated with a chondrogenic differentiation phenotype, with minimal fibrogenic influence. The proteins modulated by 02–09 correlated with a dual profile (both chondrogenic and fibrogenic potential). Our results suggest that C3 has potential as a targeted chondrogenic agent, while 02–09 may serve as a multifaceted modulator of both cartilage repair and ECM protection. These findings indicate the utility of these compounds for regenerative medicine and the development of disease-modifying therapies for inflammatory and immune-related conditions.

Materials and methods
In silico
screening of compounds.
The crystal structure of 37 LR (PDB ID:
3BCH
) was cleaned and prepared using AutoDock Vina v1.1.2 and Autodock Tools v1.5.7, as outlined in Ref. [
7
]. The Maybridge HitFinder™ version 10 library comprising 14,400 drug-like compounds was accessed using “Docking At UTMB” (now “Docking At TACC”), a virtual screening web portal that performs automated docking of pre-cleaned. Pdbqt libraries against an input structure [
8
]. The top 24 compounds (−9.3 kcal/mol to −7.9 kcal/mol) were recorded and evaluated for downstream applications, and the top one (C3) with activity in anti-inflammatory gene expression [
2
] was used in the present work. The top compounds were obtained from Maybridge via Fisher Scientific (now available from GLIXX laboratories, Inc. Hopkinton, MA). Compounds were resuspended in 100% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, Sigma Aldrich) to 10 mM and stored at −20 °C. Redocking of C3 was performed using Autodock Vina and AutodockTools and Pymol v2.2.0 used for visualization, as described [
7
].
Analog 02–09 generation and synthesis
. The synthesis of analog 02–09 was based on compound C3, involving substitution of its first aromatic ring. Both compounds share a common moiety, (4-(9H-fluoren-9-yl) piperazin-1-yl), which remained unchanged. The first aromatic ring in Compound C3 was substituted with the phenyl ring in analog 02–09. This process included the removal of the fluoro substituent, elimination of the benzo [d][1,3] dioxin ring, and the introduction of a new phenyl ring with a dimethyl aminoethoxy group. Compounds were used in culture at 10 μM (C3, 02–09, Krt) and 1 μM (peptide 18). To assess binding, we performed redocking using SwissDock, using the Attracting Cavities (AC) 2.0 mode, a recently described tool [
9
]. The SwissParam score estimates binding free energy, with more negative values indicating stronger predicted affinity; the AC score reflects how well the compound fits into prioritized binding pockets, with higher values suggesting better spatial complementarity. To validate direct interaction with the LR receptor (PDB:
3BCH
), we performed Microscale Thermophoresis (MST) using the pepG domain of LR, which confirmed binding of C3 with a dissociation constant (Kd) of ∼3 μM.
Cell Culture.
Human adipose-derived mesenchymal stromal cells (ASC) were purchased from LaCell, LLC (now Obatala, Metairie, LA) and grown on fibronectin-coated plates in MCDB-201/DMEM/10% FBS media [
10
]. Chondrogenesis assay involved seeding Passage 3–4 ASC in polypropylene tubes at 5 × 10
5
cells/tube, spun to form a pellet, then allowed to spontaneously form round mass cultures or cell pellets that received media with or without chondrogenic supplements (TGFβ-containing
Stem XVivo
media, RnD) for 21 days with media changed every 2–3 days at 5%CO
2
in a 37°C tissue culture incubator. Groups included 0.3% vehicle control (DMSO), or DMSO and each of the treatments: PEDF small peptide (p18) [
11
], Krt, or test compounds C3 or 02–09. Importantly, the StemXVivo media contains TGFβ-3, a well-established inducer of chondrogenesis known to enhance SOX9 expression and cartilage-specific matrix production.
Sample preparation
. The cells were lysed using the Barocycler NEP2320 (Pressure Biosciences, Inc.) in 50 μL of 100 mM ammonium bicarbonate at 4 °C under a pressure of 35,000 psi for 45 min. Protein isolation was performed by precipitating 100 μg of protein using acetone. Following acetone removal, the samples were subjected to reduction and alkylation, and enzymatic digestion of the extracted protein was carried out using sequence grade Lys-C/Trypsin (Promega). The digestion process took place in the Barocycler at 50 °C under a pressure of 20,000 psi for 1 h. To desalt the peptides, C18 spin columns (Pierce Biotechnology, Rockford, IL) were employed. The peptides were eluted with a solution consisting of 80% acetonitrile (ACN) and 0.1% formic acid (FA) and subsequently dried at room temperature using a vacuum concentrator for 1 h. Finally, the clean and dry peptides were resuspended in a solution containing 97% purified water, 3% ACN, and 0.1% FA, reaching a final concentration of 0.2 μg/μL.
Liquid chromatography/tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS)
. The Dionex UltiMate 3000 RSLC Nano System, coupled to the Q Exactive™ HF Hybrid Quadrupole-Orbitrap MS (Thermo Fisher Sci), was utilized for the analysis of the samples, following the protocol described in Ref. [
7
]. Data acquisition involved monitoring the top 20 precursors at a resolution of 120,000, with an injection time of 100 ms. The instrument was calibrated at the beginning of each batch run and recalibrated every 72 h using a calibration mix solution from Thermo Fisher Scientific (Waltham, MA). To ensure the instrument's performance, routine evaluations were conducted using an
E. coli
digest.
Proteomics, Metascape, Enrichr, Clustvis, and scRNAseq analyses
.
Raw files were processed using MaxQuant (
http://maxquant.org/
) version 2.1.4.0. The human proteins from UniProt (retrieved on September 18, 2022) and common contaminants were used as the sequence database. MaxQuant default settings were utilized, except for the following adjustments: “Label-free quantification” (LFQ); “Match between runs” checked; enzymes Trypsin/P and LysC; fixed modification: Iodoethanol (C). The MaxQuant result was parsed with an in-house script to remove the common contaminant proteins, extract the LFQ intensity values, and log-transformed. Missing values were imputed when all values of a treatment group were absent but present in the other group. These were filled using the lowest intensity value found in the raw dataset. A protein was defined to be differentially regulated if it reached a log
2
(FC) > 1.2 with
P
< 0.05, based on literature examples where these thresholds could conservatively identify both the changed and unchanged genes/proteins in recent studies correlating proteomic with transcriptomic changes [
12
]. Gene lists representing the proteins identified were inputted for enrichment analyses using Metascape [
13
] [accessed Dec 20, 2023]. All annotation terms were selected, membership category included all functional sets, pathways, and structural complexes. For enrichment analysis (custom) settings, a minimum overlap of 2 and p < 0.05 were selected for pathways and processes, with the PPI enrichment combined (all) databases. Cytoscape version 3.9.1 was used for the PPI image editing. Clustering analysis using comparison with Enrichr datasets used Clustvis [
14
]. Briefly, rows were centered and scaled by Pareto scaling, then clustered using correlation distance with McQuitty linkage. Columns were clustered using correlation distance and Ward linkage (unsquared distances), with values plotted as red for higher relative expression and blue for lower relative expression.
For scRNAseq analyses, we obtained a publicly available dataset (GSE1951940) [
15
] to help us determine genes associated with chondrogenic or fibrogenic phenotypes and cell populations
in vivo
. Non-hematopoietic (CD45
−
) cells were subset to focus on the fibro adipocytic/mesenchymal progenitor population, which was resolved into six distinct clusters based on UMAP and trajectory analysis using Trailmaker [
16
]. The root node, defined as CD34
+
or Ly6a
+
according to Julien et al. [
15
], represented the least differentiated progenitor state. We used the genes and cell populations identified in this dataset to correlate this average gene expression and fraction of cells expressing genes with the significantly upregulated proteins induced by C3 and 02–09 (minus or plus chondrogenic supplements) in our proteomic dataset. This orthogonal analysis resulted in a classification of proteins that correlated with a fibrogenic (F), chondrogenic (C), or fibrocartilaginous progenitor (FCP) category based on gene expression signatures from these clusters.
In vitro
data analysis
. Data are presented as mean ± SD (n = 3). Two-tailed
t
-tests were performed, with
p-value
≤ 0.05 considered statistically significant (∗).
Statistics.
All assays were run in triplicate (biological replicates,
n
= 3), with values shown as the mean ± SEM unless otherwise indicated. Student's
t
-test was used for pairwise comparisons and one-way ANOVA was used for group comparisons with significance set at
p
< 0.05. For multiple comparisons, the Holm-Sidak test or a false discovery rate was applied.

Introduction
Osteoarthritis (OA) is a prevalent joint disorder characterized by chronic inflammation and cartilage degradation. Current treatments primarily focus on pain management, lacking efficacy in halting disease progression. There is a critical need for disease-modifying therapies that can simultaneously inhibit OA-associated catabolic activity and promote anabolic processes for cartilage repair. However, promoting anabolism in OA faces challenges, primarily, reduced chondrocyte function and metabolic activity. Chondrocyte senescence is prevalent in OA, limiting regenerative potential by hindering effective cartilage repair. Additionally, age-related metabolic decline impedes anabolic processes, necessitating strategies that target cellular senescence and restore chondrocyte metabolism to enable successful anabolic therapies. This approach recognizes the crucial role of chondrocyte function and activity in promoting cartilage repair and mitigating the impact of OA.
Mesenchymal stromal cells (MSC) offer a promising solution to the challenges associated with anabolism in OA, particularly by addressing reduced chondrocyte function and metabolic activity. These regenerative cells can replace damaged chondrocytes, stimulate anabolic processes, and exhibit immunomodulatory effects, reducing inflammation in the OA microenvironment. MSC, whether sourced exogenously or endogenously, are easily isolated and expanded with a straightforward procedure, making them a practical and attractive choice for developing anabolic therapies. In particular, the accessibility and proliferative capacity of adipose-derived MSC (ASC) contribute to their widespread use in research and therapeutic applications for cartilage repair and OA treatment.
A potential target for intervention to stimulate MSC tissue regeneration in this context is the interaction between Pigment Epithelium-Derived Factor (PEDF) and the non-integrin Laminin Receptor (LR). PEDF, a glycoprotein known for its diverse biological activities, has been implicated in skeletal tissue development and differentiation. Although its exact role in skeletal tissues is not yet fully understood, studies suggest that PEDF may regulate chondrocyte and osteoblast differentiation and bone remodeling. Conversely, LR, which serves as a receptor for PEDF, is upregulated in synovial tissue and joint fluid of patients with OA and rheumatoid arthritis [
1
]. LR is involved in various cellular processes, including adhesion, migration, and signaling. Its targeting may be promising in the development of novel therapies for inflammatory conditions.
The development of small compounds that mimic the interaction between PEDF and LR has been pursued in our recent work to overcome challenges associated with the large size and low stability of PEDF. In recent studies, several small compounds were designed to bind to the docking zone of PEDF at LR, aiming to replicate the beneficial effects of PEDF [
2
]. Among these compounds, Compound 3 (C3) emerged as a very promising PEDF mimic. It effectively reduced the expression of the pro-inflammatory gene IL-1β, suggesting its potential as a therapeutic agent for OA. In our pursuit of innovative OA therapies, we extended our focus to the critical context of mesenchymal stromal cells (MSC) undergoing chondrogenesis. MSC play a pivotal role in tissue repair and regeneration, thus understanding how PEDF/LR interactions influence MSCs during chondrogenesis could provide crucial insights into OA pathogenesis, particularly in the context of cartilage repair.
The inclusion of kartogenin (Krt) [
3
], a compound with chondrogenic activity yet unrelated to the PEDF-LR interaction, offers a comparative perspective, being a molecule already under preclinical [
[4]
,
[5]
,
[6]
] and Phase I translation for OA treatment. The present work introduces the therapeutic potential of PEDF and C3 for OA treatment, with a specific emphasis on PEDF/LR interactions in MSCs undergoing chondrogenesis. These interactions offer a promising avenue for modulating inflammatory processes and promoting cartilage repair, positioning C3 as a potential disease-modifying therapy for OA.
Our commitment to developing small molecules mimicking PEDF and LR interactions led to a comprehensive analysis of compounds based on the original C3. Predictions indicated C3's interaction with Histidine-169 of the 37 kDa form of LR through a hydrogen bond, aligning with PEDF's known binding site [
7
]. Recent research explored C3's role in reducing angiogenesis [
7
], while the present work delves into global proteomics results from treating undifferentiated and differentiating adipose-derived MSC with C3 and a novel analog, 02–09. Through chemical substitution, 02–09 was developed to enhance the bioactivity and affinity of C3, aiming to further improve its therapeutic potential, particularly for rheumatic conditions. Experimental assessments involved 2D and 3D cultures of ASCs in the absence or presence of chondrogenesis stimuli, employing LC-MS/MS and mass spectrometry detection to analyze differentially expressed proteins. Comparative analysis of proteomic profiles revealed distinct patterns among ASCs treated with C3, 02–09, p18 (positive control), Krt (unrelated compound), and a vehicle control. The present study indicates promise for compounds C3 and 02–09 in contributing to the ongoing pursuit of innovative and effective treatments for OA, as examined in MSCs undergoing chondrogenesis.

Results
3.1
In silico
discovery and isolation of small compounds mimicking the PEDF-37LR interaction
To investigate the potential modulation of the interaction between pigment epithelium-derived factor (PEDF) and the 37 Laminin Receptor (LR), we conducted an
in silico
screen to discover small molecules or compounds. Previous studies have demonstrated the ability of such compounds to modulate PEDF functions or mimic the effects of a PEDF-derived peptide called
p18
[
11
,
17
]. Restoring the balance of PEDF is a desirable therapeutic approach for conditions like osteoarthritis. Therefore, our goal was to identify a small molecule that could reproduce the known signaling properties of PEDF. Using an
in silico
drug discovery strategy, we targeted the interaction interface between PEDF and LR [
7
].
To identify candidate compounds targeting LR, we initially performed docking simulations of the Maybridge HitFinder™ library against the LR crystal structure (PDB:
3BCH
) using Docking@UTMB. Twenty-four compounds were identified with predicted binding energies ranging from −9.3 to −7.9 kcal/mol. After filtering for chemical properties, top candidates were selected for in vitro testing [
7
]. Among these, compound C3 showed the strongest potential to mimic PEDF-LR interaction and was prioritized for further study. The predicted binding site corresponds to the known PEDF and laminin interaction region. We further confirmed the interaction between C3 and LR using Microscale Thermophoresis (MST) with the pepG domain, yielding a dissociation constant (Kd) of ∼3 μM.
To improve the properties of C3, we designed a second-generation analog, 02–09, by substituting its first aromatic ring with a phenyl ring bearing a dimethylaminoethoxy group (
Fig. 1
a). This strategic modification aimed to enhance hydrophobicity and cellular uptake while retaining the core pharmacophore. In parallel studies, we observed anti-inflammatory effects of C3 in THP1 macrophages [
2
], supporting its multifunctional potential. To validate binding, we performed redocking of C3 and 02–09 using SwissDock with the Attracting Cavities (AC) 2.0 mode, a recently described tool [
9
]. SwissParam scores estimate binding free energy, with more negative values indicating stronger predicted affinity, while AC scores reflect cavity fit quality. C3 showed a SwissParam score of −6.5 kcal/mol and AC score of 62.5; 02–09 showed −7.1 kcal/mol and AC score of 81.03, suggesting similar or slightly improved binding for 02–09 (
Fig. 1
b).
Fig. 1
Overview of compound discovery
from an
in silico
screen (A) highlighting compound C3 [modified from Umbaugh, 2018, under BY CC 4.0], and the structures of C3 and its analog 02–09, which are Compound C3: (4-(9H-Fluoren-9-yl)piperazin-1-yl) (6-fluoro-4H-benzo [d][1,3] dioxin-8-yl)methanone and its analog 02–09: (4-(9H-fluoren-9-yl)piperazin-1-yl) (2-(2-(dimethylamino)ethoxy)phenyl)methanone). (B) SwissDock indicating the interactions of the compounds with the RPSA/Laminin Receptor 1 molecule at His169; (C) The experimental design with adipose mesenchymal stromal cells (ASC) and proteomics workflow. Created in part with Biorender.
Fig. 1
In parallel studies, we also observed an anti-inflammatory role of
C3
in THP1 macrophages [
2
]. Considering the potential multifunctionality of compound C3, we aimed to enhance its properties by developing a second-generation molecule, termed 02–09. The analog generation involved substituting the first aromatic ring in C3 with a phenyl ring in 02–09 (
Fig. 1
a). This strategic modification aimed to optimize the compound's structure for improved functionality.
02–09
holds promise for future development as a lead compound to achieve therapeutic outcomes in conditions such as OA.
To assess the effects of C3 and
02–09
on the proteome of adipose-derived mesenchymal/stromal cells (ASC), we conducted experiments in both 2D and 3D culture environments, which promote chondrogenesis (
Fig. 1
c). We employed LC-MS/MS and mass spectrometry detection to analyze differentially expressed proteins, as described in the materials and methods section. We compared the proteomic profiles of ASC treated with vehicle (0.3% DMSO), with addition of each of the drugs (C3,
02–09
), positive PEDF-LR interacting peptide p18 (positive control), or the unrelated compound Krt. Krt is undergoing preclinical development for OA due to its recognized pro-chondrogenic properties [
[3]
,
[4]
,
[5]
].
3.2
Proteins differentially expressed in ASC with LR-targeting drugs
An analysis of the proteomics data revealed distinct patterns of protein modulation across the treatment groups. In the ASC_Proteome (
Fig. 2
a), which represents untreated ASC controls versus drug-treated ASCs, the LR-targeting drugs (C3 and 02–09) showed a greater number of upregulated proteins, whereas Krt and p18 treatments induced minimal protein modulation. Venn diagrams revealed 36 upregulated and 5 downregulated proteins shared specifically between C3 and 02–09 (
Fig. 2
a). In contrast, the
Chondro_ASC_Proteome
(
Fig. 2
b) reflects protein modulation within the chondrogenesis assay using ASC, where a larger number of differentially regulated proteins was observed. Across all treatment groups, the number of downregulated proteins remained relatively similar, while p18 treatment showed the highest count of upregulated proteins, followed by Krt and the LR-targeting drugs. Venn diagrams in this dataset identified 9 upregulated proteins common to both C3 and 02–09, as well as 9 proteins common to both drugs and p18. Additionally, 52 proteins were found to be upregulated across all treatment groups. In terms of downregulated proteins, 2 were shared between p18 and the LR-targeting drugs, and only 1 protein was common to C3 and 02–09. Moreover, 12 proteins were consistently downregulated across all treatment groups. The top 10 up-regulated proteins per group (Chondro_ASC_Proteome) were, for
02–09
: RPL35, RPL19, FABP3, ACTR1B, SAR1B, COPS3, PRMT1, PGLS, EEF1E1, MX1; for
C3
: RPL19, GNPDA1, ACTR1B, CARS2, METRNL, GOT1, COPS3, MAPRE1, FABP3, PRKAG1; for
Krt
: RPL19, COPS3, YBX3, CYP1B1, EEF1E1, PRKAG1, GNPDA1; and for
p18
: CRABP2, RPL35, SLC30A7, COPS3, ACTR1B, CARS2, YBX3, EEF1E1, MAPRE1, PRKAG1.

Overview of the differentially expressed proteins (p < 0.05) in ASC
treated with LR-targeting compounds (10 μM for C3 or 02–09), the p18 peptide control (1 μM), or Kartogenin (Krt, 10 μM), under (A) basal conditions (ASC_Proteome) and (B) chondrogenic stimulation (Chondro_ASC_Proteome). (C) Clustering analysis (Clustvis) comparing Enrichr datasets related to cartilage-specific cell or tissue signatures and processes. Upregulated protein clusters corresponding to the examined Enrichr datasets are highlighted in blue boxes. The treatment groups included C3, P18, and 02–09 (0209).
Fig. 2
Further analysis of the
Chondro_ASC_Proteome
group focused on the enrichment of chondrogenesis markers using Enrichr and Clustvis analyses (
Fig. 2
c). The results revealed distinct clustering patterns for compounds C3 and 02–09 with p18, albeit with different aspects of cell or tissue cartilage-related signatures. C3 clustered with p18 signatures related to
chondrocyte/mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) differentiation
,
alleviation of MSC aging and osteoarthritis
. On the other hand, 02–09 clustered with p18 signatures associated with
chondrocyte proliferation
,
Sox9-dependent chondrocyte development
,
cartilage fragments or post-transplant markers
,
protection of chondrocytes from the arthritogenic effects of IL-1
and showed a potential detrimental signature overlap with
negative regulation of chondrocyte differentiation
. Furthermore, 02–09 displayed additional overlap with signatures related to
chondrocyte and chondroblast differentiation
that were not observed in the other groups. P18 overlapped with
cartilage-related signatures
and
reduction of chondrocyte hypertrophy
, which were absent in the other treatment groups.

The presence of pathways related to ECM organization and the transition to chondrogenesis suggested to us that ASC may undergo a fibrogenic phase before fully differentiating into chondrocytes. The modulation of these pathways by C3 and 02–09, as well as their distinct clustering patterns in chondrogenic differentiation, supports the idea of these compounds facilitating a transition to a chondrogenic phenotype. Since we observed that C3 appears to be predominantly chondrogenic, as demonstrated by association with chondrocyte differentiation and cartilage-related pathways, it appears that the pathways enriched exhibit minimal suggestion of fibrogenic phenotype. In contrast, 02–09 displayed a dual profile, showing both chondrogenic and fibrogenic pathway-related enrichments. This could mean that 02–09 supports chondrocyte proliferation and cartilage protection, yet its involvement in ECM-related pathways and stress responses suggests a more intricate role that may also influence fibrogenic processes. While C3 shows a more pronounced chondrogenic effect, 02–09 seems to present a balanced or mixed impact on both chondrogenic and fibrogenic pathways.

Discussion
In this study, our group aimed to discover small compounds that could mimic the interaction between PEDF and the LR, testing them on undifferentiated and differentiating ASC cells. We previously conducted an
in silico
screen using docking simulations and identified several compounds, including C3, with promising potential to mimic the PEDF-LR interaction as described [
2
,
7
]. Further analysis confirmed the predicted binding state of C3 to the LR structure. While our previous study demonstrated anti-inflammatory effects of LR-targeting compounds in immune cells, particularly THP-1 differentiated into macrophages [
2
], the present work explores their impact on ASC, especially during the process of chondrogenic differentiation. This represents a novel application of LR agonism in a regenerative context, expanding the therapeutic relevance of these compounds beyond immune modulation. Further support for LR as a therapeutic target in regenerative medicine comes from literature highlighting its role in MSC adhesion, migration, and lineage commitment. LR is part of the non-integrin laminin receptor family, implicated in extracellular matrix remodeling and chondrogenic signaling [
19
]. Laminin–LR interactions are also essential for maintaining stem cell niches and promoting differentiation [
20
]. Together, these findings position LR agonism as a promising strategy for cartilage repair and tissue regeneration, distinct from our prior work in immune modulation.
To enhance the bioactivity and affinity of C3, we developed a second-generation molecule called 02–09 through chemical substitutions. The goal was to further improve its therapeutic potential, particularly in conditions like osteoarthritis. To assess the effects of C3 and 02–09 on ASC, we conducted experiments in both 2D and 3D culture environments in the absence or presence of chondrogenic stimuli. We employed LC-MS/MS detection to analyze differentially expressed proteins. The comparative proteomic profiles of ASC treated with C3, 02–09, P18 (a positive control), the unrelated compound Krt, and a vehicle control, provided insights into their molecular and functional effects. While TGFβ3 and BMP6 are widely recognized for their roles in promoting chondrogenic differentiation [
21
], our study utilized StemXVivo media containing TGFβ3 to ensure consistent and optimized induction of chondrogenesis in ASC. Krt was included as a comparator small molecule due to its translational relevance and established chondrogenic activity in preclinical and Phase I studies. This allowed us to benchmark the effects of our novel LR-targeting compounds against a clinically promising agent. The use of Krt complements the TGFβ3-based differentiation protocol and provides a relevant context for evaluating small molecule efficacy.
Analysis of the proteomics data revealed distinct patterns of protein modulation across treatment groups. C3 and 02–09 upregulated more proteins than untreated ASC controls, while Krt and p18 treatments showed minimal changes. Venn diagrams highlighted shared and unique upregulated proteins between C3, 02–09, and p18, with some overlap across all treatments. In the chondrogenesis assay, P18 had the most upregulated proteins, followed by Krt and LR-targeting drugs. Downregulated proteins were also analyzed, showing overlaps between p18, LR drugs, and minimal overlap for C3 and 02–09. Further analyses focused on the enrichment of chondrogenesis markers using
Enrichr
and
ClustVis
analyses revealed unique clustering patterns: C3 associated with
MSC differentiation
,
anti-aging
, and
osteoarthritis markers
, while 02–09 was linked to
chondrocyte proliferation
,
Sox9-dependent development
, and
protective or negative chondrocyte signatures
. P18 uniquely overlapped with markers for
cartilage protection
and
reduced chondrocyte hypertrophy
.
Proteomic and pathway enrichment analyses of
undifferentiated ASC
treated with LR-targeting compounds, p18 peptide control, or Krt revealed interesting findings. Enrichment analyses using
Metascape
identified upregulated pathways enriched by the LR-targeted drugs, with some shared between them, including
Integrin β1 signaling, ECM organization, proteoglycans, elastic fibers
, and
TGF-β signaling
. From our proteomics dataset, of particular interest were the
matrisome pathway
(a key component of the ECM), with
NABA ECM glycoproteins
and
matrisome proteins
prominently featured in the protein-protein interaction analysis. Four of these matrisome-related molecules were shared between 02 and 09 and C3, emphasizing a potential role for modulation of ECM dynamics in the compounds' mechanisms of action. C3 specifically enriched the
Nuclear Receptors pathway
, while 02–09 enriched
Laminin interactions
,
Glycosaminoglycan-related diseases
, the
Biocarta AGR pathway
,
Hallmark apical junction
, and
Adipogenesis
. Other networks included
Hallmark EMT transition
and
Integrin β1
, which overlapped across LR drugs. Transcription factor analyses indicated common regulation by SP1 and PARP1, alongside unique regulators: 02–09 enriched TWIST2, PPARG, HOXB7, EGR1, and TWIST1, while LR drugs shared STAT5B, ZID, and CEBPB. These findings suggested that the matrisome and ECM remodeling might be central elements influenced by LR-targeting drugs, contributing to pathways critical to processes such as cellular differentiation. To further support the relevance of LR-targeting in ASC, GEO2R analysis of dataset
GSE109503
[
22
] showed ∼16-fold upregulation of LAMC3 at Day 21 of chondrogenesis in human BM-MSCs, suggesting active laminin–LR signaling during cartilage lineage commitment. Building on this, we compared LR-targeting compound effects in 2D versus 3D ASC cultures. In 2D, C3 and 02–09 moderately upregulated ECM-related proteins and early chondrogenic transcription factors. In contrast, 3D cultures (especially with 02–09) showed a stronger enrichment of matrisome and cartilage-specific pathways, including significant upregulation of TMSB4X and ALYREF. These results highlight a role for examining the dimensional context when evaluating compound efficacy and support the use of 3D models for regenerative applications.
Analysis of the
downregulated proteome of undifferentiated ASC
treated with LR-targeting drugs revealed interesting results as well. The
Hallmark EMT transition
pathway was downregulated by both p18 and C3. C3 and 02–09 shared a downregulated
mRNA surveillance pathway
, while 02–09 also downregulated
Signaling by interleukins
and
NABA matrisome-associated
pathways. C3 showed downregulation in pathways like
Influenza A, platelet degranulation, apoptosis, IFN-γ responses
, and
NRF2 signaling
. The PPI network focused on cytokine signaling and proteolysis regulation. Some downregulated proteins were shared between C3, p18, and Krt, while C3 and p18 had common downregulated molecules. Unique downregulated proteins were observed for C3 and 02–09. Transcription factor analyses revealed specific regulators for each treatment group. Overall, these findings highlight how LR-targeting drugs, p18, and Krt induce distinct proteomic changes, influencing various pathways related to
cellular processes
,
ECM organization
, and
transcriptional regulation
.
In the study investigating proteomic changes and enriched pathways in
ASC during chondrogenic differentiation
treated with LR-targeting compounds, p18 peptide control, or Krt, several interesting findings were observed.
Metascape
enrichment analyses identified common pathways among the LR-targeting drugs, including
VEGFA/R2, immune cytokine signaling, IFN-γ response, ECM glycoproteins, EMT transition
, and
actin cytoskeleton regulation
. Specific pathways enriched in certain treatments included
ribosome biogenesis
and
lipid metabolism
for p18, and pathways related to
hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
and
retrograde endocannabinoid signaling
. Shared pathways included
MFAP5 effects on endothelial permeability
(C3 and p18) and
E-cadherin stabilization
(02–09 and p18). P18 uniquely affected
amino acid biosynthesis, glycolysis
, and
estrogen response
, while 02–09 influenced
GLP-1 synthesis, matrisome-associated pathways
, and
stress responses
. C3 uniquely impacted
cholesterol metabolism, Netrin-1 signaling
, and
gastric acid secretion
. Krt did not exhibit unique pathways but shared processes with p18 and LR compounds, such as
spliceosome
and
vesicle-mediated transport
. The PPI network in
chondrogenic ASC
treated with LR compounds, p18, or Krt revealed common proteins (IMP4, MCTS1, ITGA2) between p18 and LR treatments. C3 shared proteins with IMP4 and ITGA2, while 02–09 shared proteins with CLPTM1. LR compounds upregulated CEMIP, linked to
tube morphogenesis
, while C3 uniquely upregulated COX5B, SMU1, ANGPTL4, and SRPX2, associated with
DNA transcription
,
ribosome biogenesis
, and
blood vessel morphogenesis
. 02–09 uniquely upregulated TMSB4X, ALYREF, and others, influencing diverse pathways. P18 uniquely upregulated ARL3, IDH3B, and linked to membrane trafficking. Shared proteins (SERPINF1, FBN1, THBS1, etc.) were associated with ECM organization, while LR drugs and p18 clustered with specific transcription factors, indicating diverse regulatory elements for chondrogenesis. Transcription factor analysis revealed common regulation by SP1 and PARP1 in LR drug groups, with unique regulators for 02–09 (TWIST2, PPARG). To validate our findings, we compared them with a published human MSC chondrogenesis dataset. This comparison linked our results with networks identified in the Peffers study [
18
], and pathways included
cellular response to stimuli and stress
,
Cytoskeleton/Integrin β1/NABA core matrisome
, and
Hallmark EMT/Endocytosis/Tube morphogenesis
, integrated into three clusters. Overall, these pathways are potential targets for modulating inflammation, promoting tissue repair, and addressing several factors contributing to arthritis, particularly in OA. Key processes including
ribosome biogenesis, DNA transcription regulation, EMT/matrisome
, and
blood vessel morphogenesis
are crucial for cell proliferation, inflammatory response regulation, and tissue repair. Targeting these pathways may help address inflammation, aberrant angiogenesis, and repair tissue damage in arthritis, contributing to more effective treatments. Although not tested, the effects are likely reversible upon compound withdrawal due to the transient nature of small molecule signaling.
Analyzing
the downregulated proteome in ASC during chondrogenesis
showed shared pathways between C3, p18, and Krt, including ECM glycoproteins and xenobiotic metabolism. C3 showed unique pathways related to
IL-2/STAT5, 20S proteasome
, and
platelet degranulation
, while p18 and Krt shared pathways involving
class A receptors
and
proteoglycans
. The PPI networks focused on
ECM organization
and the
20S proteasome
, along with
stress
and
DNA damage
responses. A commonly downregulated protein was ECM1 in both LR-targeting compounds and p18. Specific downregulations were found for C3 (PSMA6, PSMA1, TXN, PARK7, TPI1, NUTF2, LGALS3BP, PSMB2) and 02–09 (SQSTM1, FDPS). Transcription factor enrichment analysis revealed SP1 enrichment specific to C3, while 02–09 and p18 shared ZNF394, with C3 showing unique enrichment for CBF and TCF11/MAFG. These results suggested that C3 and its analog 02–09 may offer anti-inflammatory [
2
] and pro-chondrogenic therapeutic potential, potentially serving as a multi-functional novel treatment for various inflammatory-related diseases.
The presence of pathways related to ECM organization and the transition to chondrogenesis suggested that ASC might undergo a fibrogenic phase before committing toward differentiating into chondrocytes. C3 predominantly promoted chondrogenesis, aligning with cartilage-related pathways and showing minimal fibrogenic activity. In contrast, 02–09 enhanced both chondrogenic and fibrogenic pathways, indicating a complex role in cartilage protection and ECM remodeling. Thus, C3 focused on chondrogenic outcomes, while 02–09 supported both processes. To better understand the effects of C3 and 02–09 on ASC differentiation, we compared their protein upregulation profiles with scRNA-seq data from periosteal fibro-adipogenic MSC progenitors during their transition to fibrogenesis and chondrogenesis after tibial fracture. This comparative analysis revealed distinct patterns in how C3 and 02–09 modulate proteins that may be classified into different phenotypic states. 02–09 upregulated proteins correlated mostly with cell clusters upregulating chondrogenic genes (
Fmod
,
Mrc2
, and
Gpc1
), suggesting a robust potential for cartilage formation with some influence on fibrocartilage. In contrast, the proteins upregulated by C3 were more correlated with fibrogenic or fibro-chondroprogenitor phenotypes and corresponding patterns of gene expression (
Fbln1, Angptl4)
, with moderate chondrogenic potential (
Ndufa8
). Further analysis of the upregulated proteins in C3 with differentiation supplements revealed a correlation with moderate chondrogenic (Srpx2) alongside fibrogenic markers (Cox5b, Smu1, and Angptl4). This suggested that, while C3 correlated with chondrogenic populations, its overall impact was more aligned with fibrogenic populations relative to 02–09. Proteins upregulated in 02–09 supplemented with differentiation supplements correlated more with a fibrogenic phenotype, and only modestly with chondrogenic populations, as indicated by genes like
Serpinf1
and
Txn
. Additionally, p18's protein upregulation was predominantly associated with fibrogenic cell populations but also retained elements of chondrogenic and fibrocartilage potential (
Idh3b, Ahsa1
, and
Egfr
), further supporting the mixed fibrogenic-chondrogenic potential of 02–09. These results emphasize the differential roles of C3 and 02–09, with C3 appearing to promote fibrogenic pathways with moderate chondrogenic potential, and 02–09 seemingly offering a more balanced influence to support both chondrogenic and fibrogenic processes. These findings suggest that 02–09 may hold promise as a therapeutic candidate for enhancing cartilage repair while also providing a degree of ECM protection. In contrast, C3 may be better suited for fibrogenic or fibro-chondrogenic applications, such as fibrosis or ECM remodeling.
Collectively, our analyses highlight the therapeutic potential of these compounds in different aspects of regenerative medicine. The combined findings provided a detailed molecular profiling of the effects of LR-targeting compounds on ASC undergoing chondrogenesis, offering potential avenues for developing multi-functional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs for arthritis and other inflammatory conditions.
